hints: Look at the two ends that join together, the COOH end of one amino acid and the NH2 end of the other. What small molecule is removed when they join?
Start with 0.7 nm + 0.7 nm for two amino acids end to end, then subtract the combined diameters of the atoms lost as water using the single bond values in the table.
walkthrough:
**See how the amino acid length was made**

Look at the arrow from the left H to the right H. It adds up the diameters along the backbone.

$$0.060 (H) + 0.140 (N) + 0.154 (C) + 0.154 (C) + 0.132 (O) + 0.060 (H) = 0.70 \text{ nm}$$
That matches the given 0.7 nm, so we use single bond diameters in a straight line.

**See what happens in a condensation**

A dipeptide forms by a condensation reaction between COOH and NH2. An OH is lost from one side and an H is lost from the other.

$$COOH + H-N \rightarrow C-N + H_2O$$
So the dipeptide is shorter than two full amino acids placed end to end.

**Add two, then take away water**

Two amino acids end to end would be:
$$0.7 + 0.7 = 1.4 \text{ nm}$$
The water removed has one O and two H atoms:
$$0.132 (O) + 0.060 (H) + 0.060 (H) = 0.252 \text{ nm} \approx 0.2 \text{ nm}$$
Subtract it:
$$1.4 - 0.2 = 1.2 \text{ nm}$$

options.A: Too short. It subtracts far too much, almost a whole amino acid length, but only a small water molecule is lost.
options.B: Correct. Two lengths (1.4 nm) minus the water lost (about 0.2 nm) gives about 1.2 nm for the dipeptide backbone.
options.C: This is just 0.7 + 0.7 with nothing removed. It forgets that condensation removes water when the peptide bond forms.
options.D: Too long. A dipeptide cannot be longer than two amino acids end to end, and water loss must make it shorter than 1.4 nm.
